text: This lesson is about keeping client scripts fast, safe, and off patterns the platform itself has moved away from. A client script runs on the user's browser, on the same thread that's handling clicks and typing, so anything slow in it is felt directly as lag — the fix is almost always to push real logic server-side and keep the client script's own job narrow.

Here's the wrong pattern: an onChange script instantiating GlideRecord directly against sys_user, right in the browser, then reading a manager value straight off the returned record. Since the Quebec release, client-side GlideRecord is disabled by default, for both performance and security reasons — it meant arbitrary database queries running in browser JavaScript, visible to anyone who opened dev tools and watched the traffic.

The correct replacement is GlideAjax against a Script Include, the pattern Course 5 introduced. Same onChange trigger, same end result landing in the manager field, but the actual query happens on the server, and the client only receives the finished answer through a callback function. This is the modern pattern this course expects you to default to every time you need server data from a client script.

The same philosophy applies to hiding a field. Reaching into the page with document.getElementById and setting style.display is fragile, because the rendered markup underneath isn't a documented contract — it can change between releases and between Classic UI and newer renderers like UI16 or Next Experience. g_form.setVisible does the exact same job through the stable, supported API, regardless of what the underlying HTML looks like this release.

Four habits to default to: keep client scripts light and push real logic server-side through GlideAjax; never rely on client-side GlideRecord, since it's disabled by default; prefer g_form over raw DOM access for anything touching the form; and keep onChange specifically fast, since it can fire on every keystroke-driven change during a single form-editing session, multiplying any delay across the whole experience.

Next, Lesson 9 looks at the Isolate script checkbox — the setting that decides whether a client script runs sandboxed from the rest of the page in its own iframe, or shares the page's global scope directly with every other script on it.
